Madison Mathews, an Emerson College student, said she feels comfortable walking through the area.

“Walking late at night, walking during the day, I’ve never had an issue,” Mathews said. “I’ve always felt like, even if there is something going on, somebody’s on it.”

For downtown business owners, however, the recent violence is raising concerns about perception and the potential impact on customers.

Babak Bina, who owns nearly 10 restaurants and bars in Downtown Crossing and nearby areas, said a stronger neighborhood police presence could help.

“It would be incredibly helpful to have the old-fashioned beat where someone knows all of the local troopers, they know who the characters are and they know what’s happening in the streets on a day-to-day basis,” Bina said.

Bina said Downtown Crossing remains a largely safe place to visit and spend time, but he acknowledged that violent incidents can affect how people perceive the neighborhood.

“The neighborhood is by and large a very safe neighborhood to visit and to shop at and to dine at,” Bina said. “I think certainly that it does affect public perception, and that shouldn’t necessarily be reality for us.”

Shukla said the recent violence has changed the urgency surrounding the neighborhood’s public safety concerns.

“When you start seeing violent crime showing up at your front door, that is a different kind of challenge to respond to it with urgency, which is what I think we are doing now,” Shukla said.

Flynn said he wants city leaders to provide residents with a clear plan for increased police presence and public safety as the city prepares for the return of students and a busier fall season.

news_boston.title: Surprise signatures on DA candidate's nominating papers spark controversy
news_boston.author: Matt Prichard
news_boston.summary:
Some Chelsea city councilors said they were shocked to find their names on a list of Rachael Rollins campaign signatures.

“When I heard I just said, ‘What?!'” said District 1 Chelsea City Councilor Todd Taylor.

“I was kind of surprised,” said at-large Chelsea City Councilor Leo Robinson.

The former Suffolk County District Attorney, now running for the same office, responded to reports about the signatures collected in Chelsea, which include the names of all 11 city councilors, even though some say they didn’t sign or had their name appear twice.

In an interview with NBC10 Boston Tuesday, Rollins said, of her nominating papers, “My name is on that and I’m responsible for it.”

Like other candidates, Rollins was required to gather hundreds of names to secure her spot on the September ballot as she seeks to regain her spot as Suffolk County district attorney. She’d left the role to become U.S. attorney for Massachusetts, then resigning amid a scandal.

Councilors Taylor and Robinson say the issue on the campaign paperwork was easy to spot.

“The same handwriting was all the way down the sheet,” said Taylor. “It was all the city councilors, all the school committee members, the state rep.”

“You can’t be signing anybody else’s name,” said Robinson, “It’s not appropriate.”

In our interview, Rollins was asked if she plans to review other cities where her campaign gathered signatures.

“I think that’s a good idea,” said Rollins. “My hope is the state and the cities are looking over the signatures as well.”

Despite that explanation, some state leaders are taking a closer look at the situation. During an appearance on WGBH, Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell responded to a question over whether Rollins should be removed from the ballot.

“If she fraudulently got on the ballot, yes,” Campbell said.

A representative for Secretary of State Bill Galvin wrote in a statement, “nomination papers containing signatures that are alleged to be forged or fraudulent can be referred to law enforcement for their investigation.”

Rollins says she is open to further investigation.

“I would welcome any, there needs to be transparency,” she said.

The other two Democrats in the primary race for Suffolk County district attorney also shared their thoughts on Tuesday.

The incumbent, District Attorney Kevin Hayden, wrote, “It should come as no surprise to anyone that Rachael Rollins is once again embroiled in an ethical controversy of her own making. Her career has been marked by recurring questions about her honest, her judgement, and an extraordinary refusal to accept responsibility for her own conduct.”

Linda Champion told NBC10 Boston in a statement, “The candidate should terminate her campaign. You cannot be the district attorney, the chief law enforcement officer in Suffolk County without integrity. Deflecting blame and failing to take accountability, playing the victim and finger pointing doesn’t make it right.”

The Massachusetts primary election is scheduled for Sept. 1, and mail-in ballots have already started going out to voters.

news_boston.title: Why elaborate ruse Trump used in Turkey isn't like other secret presidential trips
news_boston.author: Will Weissert | The Associated Press
news_boston.summary:
Presidents have taken secret overseas trips in the past for security reasons, with schedules and logistics kept classified until after the fact to protect the commander in chief.

But not like the one President Donald Trump took in July.

After a NATO summit in Turkey, Trump stowed away in an airport catering container to slip into another plane while Air Force One — filled with White House officials, security and support staff, and reporters — was sent into the sky essentially as a decoy, just in case Iran made good on a credible threat of an attack.

Upon stopping in Britain, Trump sneaked back aboard the presidential plane undetected and scoffed when asked about potential danger.

“If I go, you go. Right?” he told reporters — gliding past the fact that if the plane had been shot down, the president wouldn’t have been aboard.

That Trump’s whereabouts were concealed then, and for weeks afterward, is believed to be unprecedented — even in a modern world where security-related subterfuge is not uncommon.

“We have absolutely seen the president fly on unmarked or decoy planes before, into Iraq, Afghanistan, other war-zone-like places,” said Garrett M. Graff, author of “Raven Rock: The Story of the U.S. Government’s Secret Plan to Save Itself — While the Rest of Us Die.”

“But this was an ongoing secret that I don’t think we’ve ever seen before.”

The White House hasn’t denied reports, but also isn’t providing details

The president’s flight out of Turkey made headlines at the time because Trump had arrived aboard a luxury jet gifted by Qatar, which was not equipped with some of the same missile detection and countermeasure systems found on older presidential jets.

He ended up traveling in a smaller government aircraft from Turkey to the United Kingdom. There, he sneaked back onto the decoy jet, descended from the aircraft and boarded the Qatari plane.

Elections 9 hours ago

Judge bars Trump admin. from implementing order aiming to limit mail voting

Social Media Aug 11

Trump media company announces a massive loss and new turnaround effort

The White House hasn’t confirmed reporting on the extraordinary lengths officials took to protect Trump, which were first reported by The Washington Post, but administration officials haven’t denied it.

Instead, Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, relied on similar wording that he used during the trip itself. “As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats,” Cheung said in a statement Monday.

Past presidents put themselves in dangerous areas

Presidents have regularly tested the confines of their office, pushing their security advisers to visit war zones as a show of American presence and their own leadership. Usually, this happens in the form of trips that aren’t announced until the president is deemed to be out of harm’s way.

What’s different this time is that Trump was covertly separated from the rest of his travelers — including the press pool meant to provide independent coverage of the president and his actions — and, instead of informing the public about what occurred once the risk had passed, the White House still hasn’t fully revealed what took place.

Graff said the presence of the White House press corps is as much about protecting “the presidency and democracy” as it is about covering the story.

“This shows that the White House just fundamentally doesn’t understand how important that role is, for the press corps to be able to provide independent and transparent corroboration about the status and whereabouts of the president of the United States at any given moment,” he said.

Officials have gone to great lengths to keep presidents safe on covert trips before.

In 2023, a motorcade pulled away from the White House around 3:30 a.m. on a Sunday, and President Joe Biden later boarded an Air Force C-32, a modified Boeing 757 normally used for domestic trips to smaller airports, and flew to Poland. Biden then took a secret, 10-hour overnight train ride to Kyiv meant to show solidarity with Ukraine after Russia’s invasion.

A press pool at the White House had been expecting a quiet Sunday for Biden in Washington. However, two journalists went to Ukraine with him and documented the trip, capturing images of Biden and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy striding past a memorial to fallen soldiers in Ukraine’s capital as air raid sirens sounded.

In Trump’s first term, he made a secret trip to Afghanistan on Thanksgiving Day in 2019, when officials kept a separate press pool and decoy plane in Florida to maintain the illusion that the president was spending the holiday at his Mar-a-Lago estate.

Instead, Trump and another group of reporters flew to the sprawling U.S. military base at Bagram, where the president spent more than three hours on the ground serving turkey to troops, giving a speech and meeting with Afghanistan’s then-president, Ashraf Ghani, while journalists documented what was occurring.

When President George W. Bush made his first trip to Iraq in 2003, news was not released until he was in the air on the way back to the United States. President Barack Obama made a furtive nighttime visit to Afghanistan in 2010, when he was meant to be spending the weekend at Camp David. Presidents Lyndon B. Johnson and Richard Nixon visited war zones in Vietnam.

Other risky trips featured presidential subterfuge

President Bill Clinton went secretly from India to Pakistan in 2000, attempting to calm tensions in the disputed Kashmir region. He was seen talking with officials in front of a military plane that he appeared to board. Instead, Clinton ducked around the front of the aircraft to another jet parked nearby.

Both planes took off for Islamabad, as did a third jet painted with the familiar baby blue markings of Air Force One.

War with Iran 23 hours ago

Trump pivots back to sanctions for Iran as other strategies to end his war fizzle

Joe Lockhart, a White House press secretary for Clinton, noted that reporters knew the president was on one of the planes, “but not which one.” He said he and other officials had briefed the press pool ahead of time and “although they didn’t know all the details, it was made clear” that Clinton “was not going to travel on the plane they were on.”

“There was no attempt to hide anything, much less lie about it later,” Lockhart wrote on social media.

Bush was visiting an elementary school in Sarasota, Florida, during the Sept. 11 attacks in 2001, and, after all commercial air traffic was grounded, officials wanted to move him to an undisclosed location.

The full White House traveling press pool flew with Bush from Florida to Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana, where officials reduced the number of reporters and staff on the plane. Bush and the smaller traveling party next flew to Nebraska’s Offutt Air Force Base before eventually returning to Washington.

Bush’s location remained secret throughout the day. However, the White House did not suggest that the president was somewhere he was not — unlike when Trump was whisked out of Turkey.

“You can imagine the different ways that this could have gone wrong, where, for a period of time, no one would have been able to independently corroborate the status of the U.S. president, or who was in charge of the U.S. government,” Graff said. “And that’s an incredibly dangerous moment for the world.”

news_boston.title: Judge bars Trump admin. from implementing order aiming to limit mail voting
news_boston.author: Michael Casey and Nicholas Riccardi | The Associated Press
news_boston.summary:
A federal judge on Tuesday ruled against President Donald Trump’s executive order that sought to create a federal voter list and directly involve the U.S. Postal Service in election operations in a way that would limit mail voting.

U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani had already halted the order Trump signed in March, his second one attempting to set national election rules. On June 25, she sided with Democratic state attorneys general in granting summary judgment, preventing the core parts of Trump’s order from taking effect.

Tuesday’s ruling creates another legal hurdle for the Trump administration to overcome should it get the initial injunction lifted by the U.S. Supreme Court.

“That it is now less than 90 days before the November 3, 2026 midterm elections underscores the critical need for an injunction to prevent Defendants from changing election rules on the eve of the election,” she wrote.

The Trump administration in late July requested that the Supreme Court halt lower court decisions that have blocked the sweeping changes in nearly half the country.

In the latest lawsuit, Talwani, who was nominated by Democratic President Barack Obama, sided with the League of Women Voters and other voting rights groups.

Her ruling granting a preliminary injunction barred the Postal Service from taking any steps to implement the order for this year’s midterm elections. She said the administration has so far declined to defend the constitutionality of the executive order.

“The executive branch has no authority to regulate elections,” she wrote.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Donald Trump 16 hours ago

Trump took a secret flight out of Turkey in an elaborate plot to hide his location amid Iran war

Social Media Aug 11

Trump media company announces a massive loss and new turnaround effort

Vaccines Aug 10

Trump signs order calling for spacing out childhood vaccines, against medical groups' guidance

“This ruling is a victory for voters and for the Constitution,” Marcia Johnson of the League of Women Voters said in a statement. “Neither the president nor the U.S. Postal Service has the authority to rewrite election rules.”

Plaintiffs argued in two lawsuits, both filed in federal court in Boston, that the Republican president’s order should be found unconstitutional because the states and Congress, not the president, have the power to set election rules. The League of Women Voters also argued that Trump lacked the authority to issue his order and the U.S. Postal Service and other defendants lack the authority to carry it out.

Trump’s Republican administration, in its motions to dismiss the lawsuits, argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing to bring their claims. They also argued that the motions are premature and that plaintiffs lack the legal basis to bring their claim based on the Administrative Procedure Act, which governs how federal agencies develop and issue regulations.

Stephen Pezzi, a lawyer for the Trump administration, said the harms the plaintiffs referenced were subjective, because much can change with the voting list before it is made final. He also said no one would be prosecuted for violating the order.

Trump’s executive order, the second one aimed at elections during his second term, comes as he continues to suggest that there is widespread voting by noncitizens. Along with his executive orders, Trump is pushing legislation in the Republican-controlled Congress to create a proof-of-citizenship mandate. The SAVE America Act has passed the House but has stalled in the Senate.

States already have detailed processes aimed at keeping their voter rolls accurate, and voting by noncitizens has been shown to be rare. It also is a felony that can be punishable by deportation.

Trump issued the order in March after a bill he supported to overhaul voting stalled in Congress. The order would have had the federal government create a list of eligible voters and then directed the U.S. Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to those on the list. Election officials argued that it was ripe for abuse and could cause chaos, and the postal union has objected to the idea of mail carriers policing ballots.

The Postal Service had published a proposed rule required by Trump’s executive order in the Federal Register, but it was put on hold by Talwani’s first ruling.

In a separate lawsuit filed against the executive order, a federal judge in Washington in May agreed with the Trump administration that it was too early to block the order because it had yet to be implemented. That lawsuit was brought by Democratic and civil rights groups. In July, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia upheld the May ruling by U.S. District Court Judge Carl J. Nichols that said an injunction against the order was premature.

Other rulings have gone against the Trump administration’s first executive order on elections, signed just months after he took office in his second term. That order would have required people to show documents proving their citizenship when registering to vote, among other changes.

Since his 2020 presidential election loss to Democrat Joe Biden, Trump has groundlessly claimed mail voting is rife with fraud and has launched a federal investigation into that year’s vote, even though repeated audits and investigations, including ones run by Republicans, found it was free of widespread fraud. Trump also has said he wants to “take over” election administration in Democratic areas.

Riccardi reported from Denver.

news_boston.title: ICE plans to give officers gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks
news_boston.author: Ryan J. Foley | The Associated Press
news_boston.summary:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers may soon be outfitted with gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks intended to gain compliance from combative individuals.

ICE plans to spend up to $20 million to purchase thousands of “conductive distraction and de-escalation devices” for officers and agents by March, according to a notice published Monday by the Department of Homeland Security.

The devices are known as the G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, and are manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC of Lexington, Kentucky. They have been used in recent years by some jails and police departments.

DHS said Tuesday that it was working on a response to an Associated Press inquiry and offered no immediate comment. Jeff Niklaus, the founder and CEO of Compliant Technologies, wrote in an email, “Unfortunately, we are unable to speak on this subject.”

The notice said the solicitation for a no-bid contract could be published as early as Friday.

Civil rights advocates expressed alarm at the plan, saying ICE officers already face criticism for their use of force with little oversight or accountability while enforcing President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Compliant Technologies says the devices function as a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate their electrical mode. The gloves must be applied directly to someone’s skin to deliver a pain stimulus that typically helps an officer gain compliance within seconds, according to the company.

“It’s immediate and sharp, and it will distract you. I call it like a bee sting,” said John Peters, president of the Institute for the Prevention of In-Custody Deaths, who is studying how the device has been used. “If the officer is getting any type of resistance from the person, this is certainly an effective tool.”

Immigration Aug 8

ICE says it expects to equip every field officer with body cameras by the end of August

Immigration Aug 7

ICE will release body camera video only when seen in the agency's ‘best interests,' policy says

Immigration Aug 8

What to know about Trump's new attempt to limit birthright citizenship

Peters said he believed ICE’s planned purchase would likely be the largest from the company to date. He said he could envision ICE officers using the gloves to help remove uncooperative subjects from cars and houses and in and out of detention facilities.

“For smaller officers or weaker officers or older officers, I think it has a great advantage” because it can produce faster takedowns and shorten confrontations, he said.

The manufacturer warns the device should not be used as punishment, against people merely exhibiting “verbal defiance or belligerence” or on high-risk populations such as children, pregnant women or elderly or disabled people.

Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the American Civil Liberties Union, said the public should have no confidence that ICE officers will use the devices appropriately. She questioned why the devices would be necessary for civil immigration enforcement and noted those getting shocked might have no advance warning.

“ICE spent the last year showing this country they are too quick to use force. Now they will be able to deploy electric shocks with the slight push of a button that maybe nobody else can see them do,” she said. “Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public.”

Supporters say the devices are generally used in specific jail and transport situations, rather than broadly to patrol on the streets. They have been used to subdue violent suspects who are refusing to get into squad cars and inmates who are harming themselves and threatening officers, according to Compliant Technologies.

Peters said he expected the devices to be misused by a small number of employees, as with other policing technologies, but he said they are unlikely to cause injuries. He said it would be important for ICE to have robust policies and training in place.

To use the device, officers must complete a course and be recertified every two years, the manufacturer says.

news_bc.title: Boston College To Rename 245 Beacon As Hayden Hall, Establish Theatre Fund After $55 Million Gift
news_bc.author: Nikita Osadchiy
news_bc.summary:
Following a $55 million donation from the estate of the late John T. Hayden, BC ’70, Boston College will rename 245 Beacon St. in his memory and establish a new theatre fund.

“John Hayden’s gift will benefit many for generations to come,” University President Rev. Jack Butler, S.J., said in the announcement. “John’s Boston College education is manifested in this gift because it encapsulates Ignatius of Loyola’s prayer for generosity. Clearly, he was a man for others who understood what he received was meant to be shared.” 

Hayden Hall, located at 245 Beacon St., is among the newest buildings on campus. 

Opening in 2022 as the University’s 150,000-square-foot “state-of-the-art” science facility, the building houses BC’s engineering and computer science departments, as well as the Schiller Institute for Integrated Science and Society, Edmund H. Shea Jr. Center for Entrepreneurship, and the Hatchery—BC’s maker space.

The building had gone unnamed until Hayden’s gift.

Hayden Hall is now the third building to be renamed this year, after 90 St. Thomas More became Martignetti Hall and Carney Hall was renamed Cadigan Hall.

The University has secured more than $180 million in donations over the last four months alone, following a record $125 million donation from the Patrick F. Cadigan estate for Carney Hall’s renovation—set to begin in 2028. BC did not disclose the size of the donation for Martignetti Hall.

The University said Hayden’s gift is the third-largest estate gift in its history and ranks among the 10 largest ever.

“We are seeing an increase in large estate gifts—such as the recent gift from the Cadigan estate—and are grateful that so many alumni are including BC in their estate plans,” Dan D’Onofrio, interim director of advancement communications, wrote in a statement to The Heights.

While the majority of the gift is earmarked for the former 245 Beacon St., Hayden’s donation will also establish a theatre fund to support the University’s theatre department, theatrical programming, and improvements to Robsham Theater—BC’s primary stage for productions.

The fund will be endowed, meaning only its income will go to support the theatre department.

The University said Hayden had made previous donations to BC, but nothing comparable to the $55 million gift. 

“We were astonished when we learned about his generosity and have worked closely with his estate to honor John’s life and legacy in a meaningful way,” D’Onofrio wrote.

Hayden, a San Francisco Bay Area attorney and real estate investor, died of leukemia in 2024 at the age of 76. A BC alum, he grew up in Washington, D.C., where he attended St. John’s College High School. 

At St. John’s, Hayden discovered his love for theatre and appeared in several musical productions, notably as Nicely-Nicely Johnson in “Guys and Dolls.”

After graduating high school, he briefly attended Wheeling University in West Virginia before transferring to BC as a junior in 1968. 

He continued pursuing his love for theatre at BC, taking part in numerous productions on campus. Even as an adult, Hayden regularly performed on stage for 15 years. 

“He had a great singing voice and a real stage presence,” Matthew McEntee, Hayden’s friend and BC ’70, recalled. 

Now, his gift will support the institution that shaped him, McEntee shared.

“John didn’t spend money on himself—he spent it on the people and places that mattered to him,” Joseph Gillach, Hayden’s friend and trustee of his estate, said. “This gift is a reflection of what BC gave him.”

news_bc.title: Boston College Ranks No. 21 in LinkedIn’s 2026 List of Best Colleges for Long-Term Success
news_bc.author: Danica Bergen
news_bc.summary:
Boston College ranked No. 21 in LinkedIn’s 2026 list of the top 50 best colleges for long-term success—a spot above its No. 22 placement last year.

LinkedIn uses five categories of postgraduate success—job placement, internships, career success, alumni network strength, and unique fields of study—to determine its annual top 50 list. This is the second year that LinkedIn has released such a ranking.

BC ranked fifth on the list of colleges in the Boston area, trailing behind Harvard University (No. 3), the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (No. 4), Babson College (No. 13), and Tufts University (No. 18). 

BC outranked Bentley University (No. 28), as well as Northeastern University and Boston University—both of which did not appear on LinkedIn’s ranking. 

The University also notably beat out the University of Chicago (No. 24), University of California, Berkeley (No. 29), and Georgetown University (No. 32). 

Joseph Du Pont, associate vice president for career services and integrated learning, noted that BC’s emphasis on cura personalis or “care for the whole person”—a core foundation of its Jesuit education—uniquely positions its students for postgraduate success. 

“The Class of 2025 data show how much learning happens through experience to complement classroom learning: more than 80 percent of survey respondents participated in internships, community service, and student leadership, and more than half reported working on a research project with BC faculty,” Du Pont said. “That combination of learning, experience, reflection, and accompaniment is a distinctive part of a Jesuit education.”

Approximately 97 percent of the Class of 2025 were employed, enrolled in graduate school, or involved with a fellowship or volunteer experience upon graduation, according to BC’s Career Center. 

The average starting salary of graduates across all schools was $74,000—with Carroll School of Management graduates having the highest average starting salary of $85,000. 

Both figures exceed the $60,000 national median for recent college graduates in 2025, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. 

According to the Career Center, Financial Services and Accounting (33 percent), Healthcare (16 percent), and Consulting, Business Services, and Entrepreneurship (12 percent) were the most popular industries for 2025 graduates. 

LinkedIn reported that the University’s top industries for post-graduate success included capital markets, hospitals and healthcare, and technology and internet. 

Additionally, LinkedIn listed BC graduates’ most notable skills as development tools, applied psychology, and hardware design. 

Du Pont expressed appreciation for the University’s ranking but emphasized BC’s primary mission of preparing students to contribute to the broader good.

“We want students to align who they are with what they do and see themselves as called to contribute to something larger than themselves when they graduate,” Du Pont said. “That means helping them connect their education and experiences, understand how their talents and values can guide their choices, and prepare for lives of meaning and impact.”

news_bc.title: Boston College Names Corey Kelly Vice President for Student Affairs
news_bc.author: Willy Connors
news_bc.summary:
Corey Kelly, associate vice president and dean of students, was named Boston College’s next vice president for student affairs, effective Aug. 1.

“Kelly brings extensive leadership expertise in student outreach and support, campus engagement, student conduct, and restorative practice, among other critical areas,” the University release of her appointment read.

Kelly succeeds Shawna Cooper Whitehead, who departed in May to serve as president of Regis University in Denver, Colo.

Unlike Cooper Whitehead, who was tapped for the role in 2021 after serving as vice president of student services at Seton Hall University, Kelly has spent her entire 13-year career under BC’s Division of Student Affairs. 

“She is credited with helping to establish a culture of care and accountability in Student Affairs, creating student experiences that enhance belonging and wellbeing, and addressing student behavior and mental health challenges consistent with the formative values of a Jesuit, Catholic university,” the release said of Kelly.

Kelly previously served as the assistant and associate dean of students and director of student conduct, and, most recently, associate vice president and dean of students.

In an email to The Heights, Kelly wrote that her years of experience have grounded her in “the University’s mission and shared commitment to a campus community where students experience belonging, growth, and care.”

She earned her bachelor’s degree in psychology and statistics from Boston University in 2009, and then continued her education at BC, earning a master of social work degree in 2013, and completing her Ph.D. in the Lynch School of Education and Human Development in 2019.

For her doctoral dissertation, Kelly published an extensive analysis of the challenges facing administrators handling campus sexual assault (CSA) cases, and called out flaws within the current system.

“Title IX Coordinators are at the forefront of this broken multi-layer system involving the government, individual institutions, and the administrators who are charged with managing CSA,” she wrote. “This needs to change in order for universities to be able to better respond to this important problem of CSA that is plaguing campuses nationwide and to improve the safety of all students while also respecting the rights of all students.”

Her dissertation is just a preview of the challenges she’ll have to address in her new role. 

Kelly also inherits a long-running fight over LGBTQ+ student resources on campus. Despite a decades-long push for a distinct resource center, one remains absent at BC.

In 2023, after renewed momentum under Cooper Whitehead, the University incorporated LGBTQ+ resources into the Thea Bowman AHANA and Intercultural Center (BAIC), but not without pushback that temporarily halted the initial plan.

University President Rev. Jack Butler, S.J., who also assumed his role on Aug. 1, all but ruled out a standalone center at BC. 

It’s unclear how Kelly will approach these challenges, but throughout her transition she has framed her leadership around continuity and care.

“The staff in our Division bring so much expertise and intentionality to their work with students and collaboration with colleagues, and I feel fortunate to have the opportunity to lead a group of such dedicated professionals,” Kelly wrote. “Looking toward the new academic year, I am eager to connect with students and work together to grow the caring culture that makes BC so special.”

As of publication, the University has not announced Kelly’s successor, and the Dean of Students position remains vacant. 

The post Boston College Names Corey Kelly Vice President for Student Affairs appeared first on The Heights.

news_bc.title: Bob Thompson Steps Down, Francesco D’Agostino Named Interim Head Coach Five Days Before Season Begins
news_bc.author: Mac Cobb
news_bc.summary:
Boston College men’s soccer head coach Bob Thompson is stepping down, according to a statement from BC Athletics released on Monday. Associate head coach Francesco D’Agostino has been named interim head coach. 

“After a lot of prayer and conversation with my family, I’ve made the difficult decision to step away from Boston College,” Thompson said, per the release. “My time here as a coach has been one of the most rewarding experiences of my life, but right now I need to be there for my family.”

Thompson’s decision comes five days before the Eagles are set to begin their season with an exhibition game at Northeastern. D’Agostino is familiar with the program, however, and is entering his seventh season on BC’s coaching staff. 

“I have complete confidence in the culture we’ve built, the character of our players, and in Coach Francesco’s ability to guide this group forward this season,” Thompson said. 

Thompson was named BC’s head coach in January of 2020 after spending two years as an associate head coach and serving as interim head coach in 2019. The Eagles finished the 2025 season 7–9–1, with a 1–6–1 ACC record. 

Since taking over as the permanent head coach, Thompson’s teams went 28–40–20, with a 5–23–12 record in ACC play. BC’s best year under Thompson came in 2024, when the Eagles went 6–5–6 and beat No. 8 North Carolina. Thompson’s lone postseason victory came as interim head coach, when the Eagles earned a 3–0 victory over Yale in the 2019 NCAA Tournament. 

Thompson also served as an assistant coach and recruiting coordinator for the Eagles from  2012–14 and spent time on coaching staffs at UMass Lowell, Tufts, and Northeastern. 

Thompson was a star player for BC men’s soccer from 1999–2002, receiving an honorable mention All-American in 2002 and winning the Big East Tournament MVP twice. His teams won two Big East Tournament titles, made three NCAA Tournaments, and set a school record for single-season wins with 18. Thompson went on to spend two seasons in the MLS playing for the New England Revolution.

news_bc.title: Grammy-Winner Hugh Jackman To Perform at 34th Annual Pops on the Heights

news_bc.summary:
Grammy, Emmy, and Tony Award–winning actor and singer Hugh Jackman is set to perform at the 34th Annual Pops on the Heights gala on Sept. 25.

Jackman is best known for his role as Wolverine in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but he also has a decorated history in musical films such as The Greatest Showman and Les Miserables. The latter performance earned him a Golden Globe. 

Off-screen, Jackman has performed in a multitude of Broadway and West End productions, and recently held a residency at Radio City Music Hall where he hosted the one-man concert series From New York, With Love. He won a Tony award in 2004 for his role in the musical The Boy from Oz.

The annual fundraiser, also known as The Barbara and Jim Cleary Scholarship Gala, raises money for financial aid for Boston College undergraduate students. Last year’s gala raised $12.3 million.

Jackman will be joined at Pops on the Heights by Patrick Vaccariello, a longtime collaborator and music director of the annual Tony Awards. In addition to Jackman, The “Screaming Eagles” marching band, University Chorale, and Joseph Gilhooly, MCAS ’27, will accompany the Boston Pops Esplanade Orchestra, conducted by Keith Lockhart.

news_bc.title: BC To Launch New Krantz Institute for AI, Ethics, and Humanity
news_bc.author: Danica Bergen
news_bc.summary:
Boston College will launch the Krantz Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Ethics, and Humanity to leverage the University’s Jesuit teaching in the study of the technology, it announced earlier this month.

The institute is made possible by a gift from University Trustee Jason Krantz, BC ’95, and Keely Krantz, BC ’95. 

“The gift will establish the Krantz Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Ethics, and Humanity, which will utilize BC faculty, visiting scholars, and industry partners to examine AI’s long-term opportunities and impact from a humanistic perspective, while instilling BC students with the judgement, wisdom, and critical thinking necessary to help them become ethical leaders in its deployment,” the announcement read.

The University did not disclose the size of the couple’s contribution, but called it a “transformative gift.”

Jason is the executive chairman and founder of Definitive Healthcare, a publicly traded data and analytics company. He is also the managing partner and founder of Breachway Capital, a venture firm focused on B2B software, data, and AI innovation. 

“Given Boston College’s commitment to formative education and the Jesuit principles of ethical discernment, BC, in our mind, is uniquely positioned to lead the conversation about the consequences of AI, what the technology means for humanity, and how it might be best leveraged in service to others,” he said in the announcement.

Keely is the president and founder of the O’Dell Women’s Center, a nonprofit organization that provides low-income women in Western Massachusetts with access to career and education opportunities. 

“We want to see values and ethics as foundational components in how the world approaches AI and AI education,” Keely said. “Additionally, we want BC students to use their formative education and discernment skills to help lead and improve the application of AI in the future.” 

BC had already begun investing resources into the study of AI before the Krantzes’ donation. According to the announcement, the University has over 30 faculty members teaching courses concerning AI, and 11 faculty have received external AI-research grants. 

The Krantz Institute hopes to build upon the existing investment by creating internal opportunities and promoting global learning. In addition to offering internships, seed grants, and AI programs to BC students, the institute will also gather pioneering scholars for future conferences and symposia on AI and ethics. 

“Boston College and Boston in general should be the gathering place for discussions where leaders across different fields, including computer scientists, business executives, government leaders, theologians, and ethicists, come together with faculty and students to discuss the impact of this critical technology on the future of humanity,” said Jason. 

Keely added that the institute aims to place the University at the center of human-centered AI innovation. 

“The Krantz Institute aspires to be different from anything we have seen in higher education and will help position Boston College to have a global impact on the future of AI,” said Keely. 

All of BC’s nine schools will be involved in the new institute. 

According to Robert L. and Judith T. Winston Provost and Dean of Faculties David Quigley, BC is aiming to hire an executive director for the Krantz Institute in the 2026–2027 academic year.

In the interim, the institute will be led by Morrissey College of Arts and Sciences Dean Gregory Kalscheur, S.J., and Carroll School of Management John and Linda Powers Family Dean Andrew Boynton.

Kalscheur and Boynton emphasized the potential far-reaching impact of the new institute, which aims to put Catholic, Jesuit thought at the center of AI learning. 

“This investment makes more widely available our faculty’s shared work of inquiry across the disciplines in service of a more just and human future, and enhances our students’ education, helping to form women and men who are not only highly skilled, but also possess sound judgment, careful reflection, and discerning wisdom,” said Kalscheur. 

Boynton noted that the Krantzes’ generosity reflects the University’s fundamental mission. 

“When you combine our enduring motto ‘Ever to Excel’ with the generosity of alumni like Jason and Keely Krantz, Boston College becomes an unstoppable force,” said Boynton. 

The post BC To Launch New Krantz Institute for AI, Ethics, and Humanity appeared first on The Heights.

news_bc.title: 90 St. Thomas More To Become Martignetti Hall After Trustee Gift
news_bc.author: Nikita Osadchiy
news_bc.summary:
Boston College will rename 90 St. Thomas More—a sophomore residential hall located on Lower Campus—Martignetti Hall, following a donation from University alumni Beth V. Martignetti, BC ’76, and Trustee Associate Carmine A. Martignetti, BC ’76, the University announced Tuesday.

“The gift, which comes as the couple celebrates 50 years since their BC graduation, will provide unrestricted support to Boston College, allowing the University and its leadership to address its most urgent needs,” a University announcement said. “In grateful recognition of this gift, Boston College will name the residence hall located at 90 Thomas More Drive Martignetti Hall.”

The University did not disclose the size of the couple’s contribution or specify how it would be earmarked.

In the announcement, the couple thanked outgoing University President Rev. William P. Leahy, S.J., for his contributions, and expressed their enthusiasm for the continuity that his successor, Rev. Jack Butler, S.J., will bring when he steps into the role next month.

“We have so much respect for Fr. Leahy and all that he has done for Boston College, which is now among the best Universities in the country thanks to his leadership,” Beth said in the announcement. “Our appreciation doesn’t end there—we’re so delighted for the transition to Fr. Jack Butler and the continuity that he will bring.”

Leahy is set to resign on July 31 following his historic 30-year tenure.

The now-Martignetti Hall was constructed in 1993, alongside its sister residential dorm, Vanderslice Hall. The building contains 60 residential suites and can house up to 380 students, according to the University website. The hall has maintained its residential address as its title until the donation.

Carmine has been a member of the University’s board of trustees since 2015 and is the president of family-owned Martignetti Companies, a wine, spirits, and beer distributor in New England. He and his wife are residents of Chestnut Hill.

Carmine previously served as the chairman of the Tabor Academy Board of Trustees—a college preparatory boarding and day school in Marion, Mass.—from 2014 to 2021, while Beth worked as a surgical nurse at Brigham and Women’s Hospital following graduation from the University.

The Martignettis did not immediately respond to a request for comment made through their company.

news_bc.title: Reimagining Public Media: NPR’s President Talks Its Current State and Its Future
news_bc.author: Mac Cobb
news_bc.summary:
Over the past year, actions taken by President Donald Trump’s administration have framed public media’s role as a divisive and partisan issue. 

But Katherine Maher sees public media as something that should look to bridge social or political divides.

“No one puts a CNN bumper sticker on their car,” Maher said. “There is a deep, emotional relationship that people have with the idea of being someone who participates in the public media.”

Maher, who has served as the president and CEO of National Public Radio (NPR) since 2024, sat down with The Atlantic’s Evan Smith on May 29 as part of The WBUR Festival in Boston.

Before NPR, Maher was the CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation for five years and served as an adviser to the U.S. Secretary of State’s Foreign Affairs Policy Board from 2022 to 2024. 

Maher began her talk, which was moderated by Smith, by discussing the May 2025 defunding of public media by Trump and Congress, which ultimately cut $1.1 billion worth of funding to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, $120 million of which went to public radio.

“When federal funding was taken off the table by Congress in their decision last year, we knew that there would be a series of consequences,” Maher said.

Those consequences have manifested in recent weeks, as NPR has had to reduce its workforce by 36 people through layoffs, buyouts, or by leaving empty positions unfilled. But Maher is confident that those cuts will end in the near future. 

“You have to do [these cuts] in a way that prevents you from having to go back to that well,” Maher said. “Our goal was to do that. We believe we’ve accomplished that.” 

But with the American public’s trust in media at an all-time low—just 28 percent, according to a recent Gallup poll—Maher sees NPR’s preservation of local media as an important way to keep Americans trusting the news.

“Eighty-five percent of Americans think that local public, not just public media, but local media, is trustworthy and adds value to their community,” Maher said. “The presence of local media is an indicator of lower rates of polarization, greater rates of trust in democratic institutions, but also in your neighbors.” 

With this trust in mind, Maher discussed how people’s decline in radio consumption and changing work habits have forced NPR to adapt its news distribution. 

“We are moving to a model that really encourages digital engagement,” Maher said. “We need to have a digital relationship, because that is where we are today.”

She went on to acknowledge that this movement will force NPR to overcome some of the issues it has had in the past with online coverage.

“There’s a way in the past that the network competed against itself when it came to digital,” she said. “Now my view is that we have to bring everybody together into a singular platform and place where we’re able to say that, you know, all these folks may be consuming information or engaging with everything from Tiny Desk, Morning Edition to your local public affairs show, but they’re doing it in a home that feels like public radio.”

According to Maher, the goal of public media—specifically public radio—is simple: to reduce polarization and get people to recognize each other as people.

“Audio requires you to hear someone—it requires you to listen,” Maher said. “And when we do our work best, we are asking you to listen to someone who you might fundamentally disagree with and also you cannot deny their humanity. That is what public radio can do.”

news_bc.title: BC Football Countdown to Kickoff 2026: Pitt Preview
news_bc.author: Niraj Patel
news_bc.summary:
Following a bye week, next up for the Eagles is a home game against Pitt. Pitt enters 2026 as one of the ACC’s real dark horses. They have the pieces in place to contend for 8+ wins, but facing some turnover, and a defensive-staff reset. The Panthers were projected ninth in the ACC media poll, but have about the fifth best odds to win the conference outright. After winning 8 games last season largely with a promising true freshman quarterback, they are primed to continue their ascent with an exceedingly manageable schedule.

Game Notes

  • Who: Boston College vs. Pitt
  • Head Coaches: Bill O’Brien, Boston College; Pat Narduzzi, Pittsburgh
  • When: Saturday, Oct. 17 TBD
  • Where: Chestnut Hill, MA

Series History

The two teams have only faced off six times in the past 20 years with both teams winning three, each at their respective homes. Pitt dominated last year’s matchup 48-7, but BC was on top the year prior.

Pitt Panthers 2025 Recap

Pitt found their quarterback of the future in Mason Heintschel about a month into the season against none other than BC. That game was the beginning of a five-game win streak, but they did finishing losing 3-4 albeit against the likes of Notre Dame, Miami, and then East Carolina in their bowl game. The Panthers finished 8-5 and 6-2 in conference.

Offense: Mason Year 2

Heintschel enters the offseason as the clear number one guy. He completed nearly 64% of his passes and threw for 2,354 yards and 16 touchdowns to eight interceptions. The young quarterback finished 9th in the preseason Player of the Year poll as it’s clear the team he can carry this team far with his big arm. And he gets all the benefits of a veteran offensive line too. Offensive tackle Ryan Baer checks in on Bruce Feldman’s annual ‘Freaks’ List as a 6-7, 330-pounder with a motor. The 35-game starter received All-ACC Honorable mention last season as did guard BJ Williams. They add some transfer depth here to, but the consistency should help turn around the high sack allowance.

Another freshman, Ja’Kyrian Turner, led the team in rushing last season. He returns bringing his home-run ability hitting 200 yards against Georgia Tech, and gets some transfer depth to support. At receiver, Cataurus Hicks is the lone returning starter and he was only the team’s third leading receiver with 422 yards and four touchdowns. They’ll need to have guys really step up and replace production. A true freshman in Bryce Yates could be a home-run threat, and they bring in Malik Knight from Western Carolina. Oklahoma tight end Carson Kent adds to the pass catching group.

The 2025 offense put up points, but struggled on third down. With a full offseason of preparation, you have to imagine they make strides here and keep the good times rolling.

Replacing Defensive Production

The biggest roster question is whether Pitt can replace the production and leadership of departed second-team All-ACC linebackers Kyle Louis and Rasheem Biles. Biles transferred to Texas after leading the 2025 team in tackles, tackles for loss, and defensive touchdowns, while Louis goes to the NFL after racking up 81 tackles, 8.5 TFL and three sacks. Senior Braylan Lovelace is the returning centerpiece for the linebacking corps. He’s a preseason All-ACC player, and is joined by a pair of transfers to retool, namely Alex Sanford from Purdue to play in the Biles role outside.

Up front, Narduzzi’s team should continue to be steadfast despite losing their stud defensive tackle to Notre Dame. Jimmy Scott and Isaiah Neal combined for eight sacks and they still have a stout interior of veterans and bring in some transfer depth. They fielded one of the better run defenses, and should continue to be aggressive up front.

They’ll have to improve in the secondary, but they do bring in a corner Raion Strader from Auburn. Strader returns home after a few stops. Longtime secondary coach Cory Sanders was promoted to defensive coordinator for this season and will have a few new assistants in the mix.

Matchup Preview

This is the crossroads of the BC season. They should certainly keep things more competitive than last year’s drubbing. With a bye week to prepare and with Pitt having to take a trip to Miami next week, this game sets up nicely. There’s only a couple ‘winnable’ games in the back half of the season, so it feels like a kitchen sink sort of effort.

news_bc.title: BC Football Countdown to Kickoff 2026: Virginia Tech Preview
news_bc.author: Joseph Celia
news_bc.summary:
The Boston College Eagles welcome the Virginia Tech Hokies in their third straight home game.

Game Notes

  • Who: Boston College vs. Virginia Tech
  • Head Coaches: Bill O’Brien, Boston College; James Franklin, Virginia Tech
  • When: Saturday, September 26 (time TBD)
  • Where: Chestnut Hill, MA

Series History

The Eagles have not won a game versus Virginia Tech since 2021. The Hokies have had their number of late, as they’ve beaten the BC in four of the last five contests. The Eagles have an 11-22 record vs the Hokies in their all time matchups, dating back to 1993. Down below are the last five results between the two squads – and it’s not exactly pretty. 

  • 10/17/2020: VT 40, BC 14 (Away)
  • 11/5/2021: BC 17, VT 3 (Home)
  • 9/10/2022: VT 27, BC 10 (Away)
  • 11/11/2023: VT 48, BC 22 (Home)
  • 10/17/2024: VT 42, BC 21 (Away)

VT 2025 Recap

After starting out 0-3, head coach Brent Pry was fired following the team’s poor start. James Franklin replaced the former head coach in November. While they finished 3-9 in the ACC, interim head coach Philip Montgomery helped steered the ship in a positive trending direction for 2026.

2026 Outlook: Offense 

VT currently has a QB competition between Ethan Grunkemeyer and Bryce Baker, the former starting multiple games for the Hokies last season. Grunkemeyer comes from Penn State, who has the experience advantage in Coach Franklin’s system vs Baker. Baker has not played a single snap at the college level, but is a four star prospect with a solid high school football resume. By the time the Eagles and Hokies meet there is no question that one of the two QB’s will have solidified the starting play calling job. 

The offensive weapons are decent for VT, but not anything spectacular. Running back Marcellous Hawkins returns, following a strong 2025 season in which he ran for 749 yards and 1 TD while averaging 6.3 yards per carry. The lack of touchdowns is a concern, but he has a clear path of being the bellcow of their offense with Terion Stewart now wearing a Kansas City Chiefs uniform. The other focal point of the offense is Luke Reynolds. Reynolds, a Tight End, showed promise in 2025. The numbers aren’t eye popping as he only caught 26 passes for 257 yards last season, but he is expected to have a much bigger role in 2026. 

The Hokies offensive line is still a work in progress. It was nothing short of rough in 2025, as inexperience negatively cost them. They are bringing back most of the O Line from last season, in hopes that the offseason programs and camps will pay dividends and develop their guards, tackles, and centers. 

2026 Outlook: Defense

Despite firing Pry just three games into last season, the Hokies elected to bring him back as their defensive coordinator. He brings in a new defensive line coach in Sean Spencer, whom he coached with during his days at Penn State. 

The interior defense will look vastly different versus last year’s squad. They lost a lot of players from graduation and the transfer portal, so fresh new faces are what’ll define their defense – for better or for worse. Notable names for the Hokies defensive line includes: DE Kemari Copeland, NT Emmett Laws, DE Elhadj Fall, and LB Kaleb Spencer. 

The secondary is more established for VT. Returning CB’s include Joshua Clarke, Isaiah Brown-Murray, and Thomas Williams. They bring in transfers Cam Chadwick of UConn, and Jacquez White of Troy for depth. Safety Tyson Flowers returns after a strong 2025, along with Quinton Reddish returning after missing most of last year with injury. 

Matchup versus Boston College

It’s tough to gauge exactly how this matchup fares for the Eagles. One thing to remember is they play the Hokies in the earlier portion of the season schedule, so it may take a while for VT to get their legs going. Then again, the same could be said for BC. VT is looking to bounce back following a bad 2025, and their talent simply outmatches the Eagles in many areas. The Eagles may make things interesting, but VT should win this game.

news_bc.title: Boston College Great Signs Massive Extension With Baltimore Ravens
news_bc.author: Greg Patuto
news_bc.summary:
Zay Flowers spent four years dominating the ACC for Boston College and has been doing the same at the next level.

On Tuesday, the Baltimore Ravens inked Flowers to a four-year extension worth $140 million with $108 guaranteed. This contract has Flowers behind only Jaxon Smith-Njigba ($42.15 million) and Drake London ($35 million) in terms of annual salary.

The 25-year-old receiver was under control through 2027 after the Ravens exercised his fifth-year option. The two sides decided to get a new deal done and extend the arrangement four more years.

Flowers became the first Ravens’ receiver in franchise history to be selected to the Pro Bowl in 2024. He caight 74 passes for 1,059 yards and four touchdowns. In 2025, he took steps forward with 86 catches, 1,211 yards and five touchdowns.

Baltimore selected Flowers with the 22nd-overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft out of Boston College.

Flowers left Boston College as the program’s all-time leader in receiving yards (3,056) and receiving touchdowns (29). He is also second all-time in catchers with 200, behind only Lewis Bond. Flowers led the ACC in receiving touchdowns in 2020 and 2022. In his senior year, he finished with 78 catches for 1,077 yards and 12 touchdowns.

news_bc.title: Boston College Makes Cut For Major Targets In 2027-28
news_bc.author: Greg Patuto
news_bc.summary:
Boston College has been busy on the recruiting front to prepare for the winter.

In recent weeks, the Eagles have received good news on some top targets over the next two years.

It began with four-star guard Antonio Pemberton. On Wednesday, Pemberton narrowed his list down to eight teams. There will be more cutdowns in the future but for now, Boston College remains in the mix.

The Eagles were featured on the list with UCLA, Creighton, Marquette, Tennessee, Ohio State, Kansas, and Michigan.

Pemberton is currently ranked as the top player in Massachusetts. Nationally, he is the No. 8 point guard and No. 33 player, according to 247Sports. Pemberton played for Mass Rivals AAU on the 3SSB circuit, where he scored 24 points per game on his way to Offensive MVP honors.

Last week, four-star point guard Tre Keith announced his final six schools. Boston College remains in the mix along with Clemson, Georgia Tech, Mississippi State, St. Louis, and Virginia Tech.

The 6-foot-2 guard is rising fast in the 2027 class. He is currently ranked as the No. 6 player in Georgia and No. 60 in the nation, according to 247Sports.

Keith, who is a product of Tri-Cities High School in Atlanta, has been climbing up rankings due to his ability on the offensive end of the floor. He made a major impact on the 3SSB circuit this summer, averaging 20.3 points per game for the AE5 team.

Keith has an official visit to Boston College scheduled for Sept. 25. This will be his second visit, two weeks after visiting Clemson.

Boston College Getting Jump on 2028

The Eagles are looking ahead to the 2028 class as well.

Four-star forward Payton Wilson continues to gain attention as he heads into his junior year. He is currently ranked as the No. 1 overall player in New York.

Wilson has become known for his motor on both ends of the floor. He turned in double-doubles during the Nike EYBL Peach Jam while also receiving invites from the Nike Elite 100 and Pangos All-American Camp.

Wilson shared that he is considering Boston College, Notre Dame, and Utah early in his recruitment. He holds offers from Seton Hall, UAB, and St. Bonaventure but it is likely that many more will be coming.

news_bc.title: BC Football Countdown to Kickoff 2026: SMU Preview
news_bc.author: Greg Patuto
news_bc.summary:
The schedule continues into October with Boston College hitting the road to go South and take on SMU in Week 5.

Game Notes

  • Who: SMU Mustangs vs. Boston College Eagles
  • Head Coach: Rhett Lashlee
  • When: Saturday, Oct. 3
  • Where: Gerald J. Ford Stadium in Dallas, TX

Series History

This matchup has not favored Boston College. While there is not much history there, the Eagles are just 1-3 against SMU all-time. These teams have played in each of the last three years with SMU winning two in a row. The first meeting came 40 years ago in University Park, Texas.

  • 10/4/1986: SMU 31, Boston College 29
  • 12/28/2023: Boston College 23, SMU 14
  • 11/16/2024: SMU 38, Boston College 28
  • 11/8/2025: SMU 45, Boston College 13

SMU 2025 Recap

SMU finished with a record of 9-4 last season and 6-2 in conference play. The Mustangs reached as high as No. 16 in the AP Poll, which was their mark to begin the season after back-to-back 11-win campaigns. The season ended with a 24-19 win over Arizona in the Holiday Bowl.

Kevin Jennings returned as the starting quarterback after leading SMU to the College Football Playoff in 2024. He led the ACC with 13 interceptions.

Let’s face it, the losses were ugly. SMU was upset in a shootout against Baylor in Week 2 last season, 48-45. The Mustangs would go on to lose a 13-12 rock fight against Wake Forest at the end of October. SMU earned a statement win against Miami to begin November and did not let down the next week against Boston College. The regular season ended with a 38-35 win over Cal.

Offense: Kevin Jennings leads an absolute unit

SMU has turned into a power in the ACC and the return of Kevin Jennings should keep it that way.

Despite struggling with interceptions last year, Jennings has been dynamic with 59 total touchdowns over the last two years. He has the talent and experience necessary to take the offense to the next level — and he has plenty to work with.

The Mustangs return PJ Williams at tackle along with 320-pound Dramodd Odoms on the other side. Addison Nichols and Joshua Bates are other massive bodies on the interior that bring experience. Kendrick Raphael, who tore up SMU last year at Cal, committed in the transfer portal and will now work with Derrick McFall in a talented backfield.

If there is a negative, along with Jennings’ ACC-leading interception number, it is the group of wideouts. Yannick Smith comes in from East Carolina to join Yamir Knight. Jalen Cooper will need to take a big step forward to help the pass catchers.

Defense: Transfers at front of rebuild

The Mustangs did work in the transfer portal this offseason to rebuild the defensive side of the ball.

Malcolm Alcorn-Crowder from Kansas State leads the way in the front seven as an immediate starter. This will help Marques White and Ira Singleton on the edges get to the quarterback. As good as the defensive line can be, the linebackers are among the ACC’s best.

Brandon Booker and Alexander Kilgore were major contributors last season while Jamal Anderson transferred in from Clemson.

In the secondary, Jarvis Lee and Jayvon Thomas come in with Jimmy Wyrick, who totaled 62 tackles and eight passes defended at UTSA in 2025.

Matchup Preview

A 45-13 beatdown at the hands of the Mustangs last season does not instill much confidence this time around — and it will be on the road. This game is early but not early enough to think about a potential upset spot. Boston College will enter as underdogs once again against an SMU team that will have a few weeks under its belt to gel. If the Eagles want to be able to hang around here, it will be on the defense. It is unknown if the Eagles will be able to score with Jennings and the Mustangs offense. Maybe force a few turnovers to keep it close in the second half?

news_bc.title: Bill O’Brien Makes List Of Coaches On Hot Seat In 2026
news_bc.author: Greg Patuto
news_bc.summary:
There are many head coaches that will be put under a microscope this fall.

The 2026 season will be very telling for many in the Power Four ranks. Coming off a two-win season, it is not surprising to hear Bill O’Brien in conversations surrounding coaches on the hot seat.

In a recent list put together by Sports Illustrated, O’Brien was featured on a top five list on which coaches are on the hottest seat entering the season.

“Aside from the defensive backfield, there is turnover across much of Boston College’s 2026 roster. The Eagles are likely to trot out Mason McKenzie at quarterback, a Division II transfer from Saginaw Valley State. A schedule that features three Power Four non-conference bouts and several upper-echelon ACC programs leaves little room for growth.” — Tucker Harlin, On SI

Bill O’Brien took over for Jeff Hafley at Boston College in 2024. This came after a long stretch in the NFL followed by two years as Alabama’s offensive coordinator.

The Eagles finished 7-6 in year one under O’Brien, reaching as high as No. 24 in the AP Poll. Year two saw a major regression as Boston College went 2-10 in 2025.

The upcoming season will be important for O’Brien to prove to the program that he is the right man to lead the team moving forward.

news_bc.title: BC Football Countdown to Kickoff 2026: Rutgers Preview
news_bc.author: Niraj Patel
news_bc.summary:
Boston College’s home opener will be against Rutgers. The game will feature as Red Bandana Game and will actually be played on the 25th anniversary of 9/11 and Welles Crowther’s passing. The game will be nationally televised on ESPN2.

Last season’s starting quarterback Dylan Lonergan will also make his return with his new team. He started the 2025 season with such promise, but quickly faltered. He’s still in a bit of quarterback competition, but will hope his third stop will see more success.

Game Notes

  • Who: Boston College vs. Rutgers
  • Head Coaches: Bill O’Brien, Boston College; Greg Schiano, Rutgers
  • When: Friday, September 11 at 7:30pm
  • Where: Chestnut Hill, MA

Series History

The Eagle still lead their old Big East compatriots 20-7-1, with 10 wins at home and away. Rutgers did however snap an 11 game winless stretch with the most recent matchup 22-21 at Alumni Stadium to start the 2022 season.

Scarlet Knights 2025 Recap

Schiano’s team took a step back last season, missing out on a bowl game and going 5-7 overall and 2-7 in conference. They took care of business early, but endured some narrow losses to the likes of Iowa, Minnesota, and Penn State that put a damper on the season beyond the expected blowout losses to Oregon and Ohio State. Late-game execution and defensive breakdowns were a constant headache and not typical of a Greg Schiano team. On the positive, the offense was surprisingly explosive and the team finished fifth in the nation in fewest penalty yards. Although quarterback QB Athan Kaliakmanis was drafted in the 7th round, they still return a lot of their most productive offensive players and will try to replicate that output while cleaning up those defensive woes.

Can the offense do it again?

Junior running back Antwan Raymond and 6-6 junior wideout KJ Duff are looked at among the best in the Big Ten. Raymond was the focal point of the ground game, handling the majority of carries running over 5 yards a cli. He finished nearly 1500 yards from scrimmage and a team-leading 15 touchdowns, while being named Second Team All-Conference. Duff joined Raymond on the Second Team, eclipsing 1000 yards as well to go with seven scores. Both find themselves on Preseason All-America lists for the upcoming year. These two will be a real handful.

Overall offense was remarkably efficient, featuring a wide-open passing game, strong red-zone effectiveness from Raymond, and avoided turnovers. The door is open for Dylan Lonergan to take over and keep the ship afloat, but he does appear to still be in a bit of quarterback competition with redshirt sophomore AJ Surace who saw some action last season. The pieces around them are good. The team also returns a few key lineman particularly on the interior, but must replace the tackles. Pass protection left a lot to be desired, so if they can shore that up so Lonergan can keep his much-needed clean pocket, they can replicate some of their success.

Will the defense turn it around?

Schiano will look to restore his defensive reputation after a disappointing campaign in which they were ranked 127th overall. He started by firing nearly the entire defensive staff and brought in South Dakota’s Head Coach Travis Johansen to be his defensive coordinator.

Up front, the team returns most of their interior defensive line and adds a few productive transfers to bolster the rotation. The front saw a fair amount of injuries that made things even more difficult, but among their big issues was getting to the quarterback, posting just 11 sacks with no one even getting to three sacks. Transfers Malachi Davis (Toledo) and J’Dan Burnett (Tulsa) combined for 12 last season. On top of that, the run defense was dismal allowing over 210 yards per game, sixth worst in the FBS and 33 ypg worse than BC. In comes a new tackle and another back from injury, but it will take a lot to clean this up. Most of the key linebackers return and they add in a couple transfers here to make for a really deep corps.

In the secondary, they found three new potential starters in the transfer portal, including an FCS All-American. Last year’s team was porous and only posted 5 interceptions, and they still lost their best corner to Texas. There are still question marks here with all the new faces and a pretty open competition. Schiano’s helped develop some great players over the years, and it won’t take much to get back to their average output from the previous four seasons.

Matchup Preview

Both teams have questions at how their quarterbacks will play, but Rutgers seems to have a lot fewer question marks than BC. With their returning output on offense, they should have the edge early in the season. You have to think Schiano’s defense will make strides, but hopefully the unknown element Mason McKenzie brings to the offense can create more challenges.

The Rutgers loss in 2022 was a harbinger of doom for the Eagles that year. This time we’ll have our feet wet already and won’t have to think ahead with Maine the following week. Rutgers meanwhile starts with UMass but has a date with USC after this one. This being the Red Bandana Game will add an extra energy. The Eagles will pick up their first win of the season here.

news_bc.title: BC Football Countdown to Kickoff 2026: Cincinnati Preview
news_bc.author: Greg Patuto
news_bc.summary:
Boston College is looking to improve off a two-win campaign in 2025.

The Eagles will travel to take on Cincinnati to begin the 2026 season this September.

Game Notes

  • Who: Boston College vs. Cincinnati
  • Head Coaches: Bill O’Brien, Boston College; Scott Satterfield, Cincinnati
  • When: Saturday, September 5 at 3:30pm
  • Where: Nippert Stadium in Cincinnati, Ohio

Series History

These teams have met eight times in their history with the first coming in 1961. They have split these eight meetings, 4-4. Boston College won the first two meetings without allowing a point. Cincinnati got the best of the Eagles in their last game played in 2020.

  • 9/23/1961 – Boston College 23, Cincinnati 0
  • 10/17/1964 – Boston College 10, Cincinnati 0
  • 11/4/1967 – Cincinnati 27, Boston College 21
  • 10/26/1985 – Cincinnati 24, Boston College 17
  • 9/10/1988 – Boston College 41, Cincinnati 7
  • 10/12/1996 – Boston College 24, Cincinnati 17
  • 9/27/1997 – Cincinnati 24, Boston College 6
  • 1/2/2020 – Cincinnati 38, Boston College 6

Cincinnati 2025 Recap

It was a quick start for Cincinnati in 2025. After a season-opening loss to Nebraska, the Bearcats would win seven games in a row including a 5-0 start in Big 12 play. Cincinnati sat at 7-1 with victories over Iowa State, Kansas, and Baylor.

The final third of the season was not kind to Cincinnati. It finished the season with four straight losses against Utah, Arizona, BYU, and TCU. The Bearcats ended the regular season with a record of 7-5 and 5-4 in conference play. Cincinnati was selected for the Autozone Libert Bowl, which was a 35-13 loss to Navy.

Offense: Can new QB continue momentum?

Brendan Sorsby is gone. The former Bearcat was one of the biggest names in the transfer portal before landing at Texas Tech, and whatever else. This means Cincinnati had to hit the portal to land Georgia Southern transfer JC French IV to take over under center.

The question is — can French IV air it out like Sorsby?

Cincinnati moved fast last year and got it done through the air, which led to victories. The Bearcats went 6-0 when averaging ver 8.5 yards per completion. This year, French IV has plenty of wide outs to work with who expect to put up big numbers.

Despite the loss of Cyrus Allen, the Bearcats have an impressive group built through the transfer portal. JV Gibson comes over from Oklahoma along with Larenzo Fenner, Cade Wolford, and Flynn Schele. All are expected to play pivotal roles on the outside.

In the backfield, it’s Zion Johnson who is prepared to break out. French IV is a capable runner as well and this gives the team a dual-threat option.

The other question is — can Cincinnati score against big-time opponents?

The Bearcats got off to that quick start to the season thanks to the offense before being slowed down drastically over the final four games. This is where French IV will have to help the offense take that next step.

Defense: Can it survive being on the field so much?

The flipside to the offense moving quickly is that the defense has to be on the field more. Last year, that hit a wall toward the end of the season and it showed. This year, is the defense prepared for the challenge?

Nate Woody comes in as the defensive coordinator to help fix different issues. Two major transfers on that side of the ball include Chidera Otutu and Josh Hough, who are both expected to make an impact along the defensive line. The Bearcats do not feature that premiere pash rusher so it will need to rely on its depth to get in the backfield.

Another way to offset the speed of the offense is for the defense to get off the field. The Bearcats struggled with this at times, especially when forcing turnovers. Cincinnati came away with just two interceptions on 389 pass attempts by opponents. Cincinnati was also last in the Big 12 in first downs allowed.

Matchup Preview

According to multiple sites, Boston College currently sits as a touchdown underdog in the opener on the road against the Bearcats. While there is a chance that it moves either way before kickoff, that feels about right. It is also not an impossible upset for the Eagles to pull off but it will be an uphill battle. There are many changes on both sides of the ball for both teams but the tempo of Cincinnati can be a bother for opposing defenses. The other angle of this is can Boston College take advantage of some of the Bearcat struggles defensively from last season?

This will ultimately be the decider. Can the Eagles get in the win column early with a statement victory in Week 1?

Democratic socialist Francesca Hong loses Wisconsin governor’s primary despite leading in polls, a setback for the surging movement

Hong, a state lawmaker and former restaurant owner, narrowly lost to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley after an unexpectedly close primary. She had promised to put a hold on building data centers, impose higher taxes on millionaires and set up public grocery stores.
